posts.title: Let an AI agent tend a shared garden
posts.promise: Try a tiny scheduled garden update, with a person checking every change.
posts.whatItIs: AI Zen Garden is an interactive field of raked sand and objects. A visitor can claim a plot using email and fill it by hand or let their own AI agent tend it over MCP, a way for software to communicate with tools. A beginner could test a small scheduled update to a personal plot; that experiment is a proposal, not a demonstrated customer service.
posts.whoPays: Hypothesis: people who want a personal, AI-maintained garden might pay for a service that prepares and schedules plot updates. The source gives no evidence of paying customers.
loop: A person chooses one small garden change, such as adding an object (illustrative example).
The agent prepares a proposed update for the person's plot.
A scheduled task can submit an addition to the plot, as the site describes for Claude tasks.
The person reviews the public plot and decides whether to keep or remove the change.
posts.evidence: The site describes an endless raked-sand field, plots claimed by email, hand or AI-agent tending over MCP, and scheduling a Claude task to add something to a plot. It says everything made is public.
posts.uncertainty: The source does not show whether scheduled updates work reliably or establish demand or revenue. The proposed agent must have access only to the user's plot; a person should review proposed content and remember that the result is public.
first24Hours: Read the site's terms and privacy information and confirm what making a plot public means.
Claim a plot with an email address and try one manual change.
Sketch one scheduled agent update and a human review step before enabling it.

ease.reason: A beginner can claim a plot and make a manual change, but the source gives no setup details for the proposed agent experiment.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: garden users might pay for prepared updates, but the source provides no buyer or payment evidence.

feasibility.reason: A small scheduled plot update is bounded, though agent setup and safe handling of a public plot remain obstacles.

autonomy.reason: The site describes scheduled Claude tasks adding to a plot; choosing and reviewing public changes remains human work.

evidence.reason: First-party site text describes the working garden, plot claim flow, agent tending, and scheduling example, without verified use outcomes.

posts.title: Build a small workflow with readable markup
posts.promise: Explore a workflow that keeps steps visible and leaves decisions for human review.
posts.whatItIs: WOML is an open-source language and runtime for automated workflows, apps, and AI agents. Its source describes readable markup for structure, JavaScript for logic, and a runtime that handles attempts, retries, waits, recovery, and execution history. A beginner could adapt an example into a small workflow that drafts a result for review; that is a proposed exercise.
posts.whoPays: Hypothesis: a small team building internal workflows might pay for help setting up or adapting one. The attached source does not establish customer demand or revenue.
loop: Choose one simple workflow and identify the input and desired draft output (design choice).
Write visible trigger and step structure in a WOML file.
Add JavaScript logic only for the needed transformation.
Let the runtime execute and keep its state and execution history.
Show the draft result to a person, who checks it before any consequential action.
posts.evidence: The repository describes WOML as an open-source code-first language and runtime, with readable workflow structure, JavaScript logic, and runtime support for attempts, retries, state, waits, recovery, and execution history.
posts.uncertainty: The attached excerpt describes capabilities but does not establish how easy a first workflow is, or show a real user's outcome. A human should review outputs and approve external or consequential actions; workflow retries do not establish correctness.
first24Hours: Read the WOML README section describing its workflow structure and runtime.
Choose a harmless input and write down one draft output a workflow could produce.
Map the trigger, steps, and human approval point before implementing anything.

ease.reason: The source says markup uses JavaScript for logic, so a beginner can inspect the structure but may need coding skills to build a workflow.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: teams may pay for workflow setup, but the source gives no customer demand or payment evidence.

feasibility.reason: A tiny draft-only workflow is limited in scope, while setup and JavaScript logic are unresolved beginner obstacles.

autonomy.reason: The runtime handles execution, retries, waits, and history; a person still needs to check outputs and approve consequential actions.

evidence.reason: The first-party repository describes the language and runtime capabilities, but this excerpt has no concrete independent use evidence.

posts.title: Turn an error report into a reviewed code change
posts.promise: Let a coding agent inspect captured error evidence and propose a change for review.
posts.whatItIs: BugTape is an error-tracking product that captures supported browser errors, failed requests, and server error context, then makes evidence available to a coding agent over MCP. Its described flow lets an authorized agent investigate and open a pull request. A beginner could try the flow on a small app and review the proposed change; the test customer and adaptation are hypothetical.
posts.whoPays: Hypothesis: developers or teams maintaining web apps might pay to help investigate production errors. The attached site lists a free plan and a $29-per-month Pro plan, but does not establish customer demand or earnings for an adaptation.
loop: Set up a project and choose capture settings for a small app.
Install the relevant SDK and send a test report, as the site describes.
When a supported error is captured, inspect its available request, console, replay, and stack context.
Authorize a coding agent to read the evidence over MCP and propose a change.
A person checks the evidence and code, runs appropriate verification, and decides whether to accept the pull request.
posts.evidence: BugTape's site describes browser, Node.js, and Python capture options; agent access over MCP; a workflow from captured error to pull request; and says the user reviews the change. It also states request and response bodies are not captured, inputs are masked by default, and visible page text can still be recorded.
posts.uncertainty: The source describes product capabilities, not proof that an agent's diagnosis or code change is correct. Capture depends on settings and event; replay can be unavailable, and visible page text may be recorded. A human must inspect privacy settings and review and verify every proposed fix before merging.
first24Hours: Read the platform limits and privacy details for the app type you would test.
Use the live demo or a small test project to inspect what an error report contains.
Write a checklist for reviewing a proposed code change before accepting it.

ease.reason: The site gives a setup command and test-report path, but requires app instrumentation and browser access approval.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: developers might pay for error investigation support; the listed product plans do not show demand for this proposed service.

feasibility.reason: A test flow from error capture to reviewed proposal is bounded, though app setup, privacy settings, and change verification take work.

autonomy.reason: Capture and agent access can automate evidence gathering and a draft pull request; the site explicitly leaves review to a person.

evidence.reason: The first-party site describes product setup, capture limits, a live demo, and the agent pull-request flow, but not independently verified outcomes.
